newsitem.title: USA: NBA basketball-PICK AND ROLL NOT OUR BREAD AND BUTTER, SAY JAZZ.
newsitem.headline: NBA basketball-PICK AND ROLL NOT OUR BREAD AND BUTTER, SAY JAZZ.

text.p: Everybody knows that the bread and butter play of the Utah Jazz, honed to perfection over the years by John Stockton and Karl Malone, is the pick and roll. Right? Wrong, according to the Jazz themselves.
At practice Tuesday for Wednesday's Game 2 of the NBA Finals, Stockton got almost testy when asked about the pick and roll. "I can't say this enough," the Utah point guard said.

"It is not the only play that we run. We run a variety of plays and I do not even know if that is our bread and butter. It is certainly something that we can go to and have confidence in. I do not think that it is close to our major play."
His coach sounded the same. "We have other things we do besides the pick and roll," said Jerry Sloan. "It isn't really our bread and butter. We try and go inside."

In their Game 1 loss to the Chicago Bulls, Sloan said, "We didn't do a good job of getting inside and they did a great job of keeping it out of there. They are tough to throw around. They are quicker, taller and longer than some of the players you play against and it is tougher to get it inside."
But those pesky reporters keep asking about the pick and roll.

It is such a simple old play: the ballhandler (say, alltime assists leader Stockton) runs his defender into the body, preferably large, of a teammate (say, the massive Malone) and then either passes to the pick-setter cutting to the basket (the classic option), dishes to someone else, or finds a shot for himself.
So why are teams still unable to defend against it, Stockton was asked.

"People can defend against it," Stockton replied. "We do not run it every play. Like any other play it is not going to work if everybody in the building knows what you are going to do and you run it every time.
"Like Karl mentioned, there are a lot of options to it. We need other players on the floor to get in the right positions and make shots when they get it."
Malone earlier had been asked what made the pick and roll so effective. "This guy right here," he said, pointing to Stockton.

"We have a lot of faith and a lot of confidence in each other. It is kind of like we know what each other is going to do beforehand and we do not talk a lot about it. That is something that we have always gone to. There are also a lot of options off of it, too. It comes from years and years of practicing with Stockton."
Chicago hero Michael Jordan had nothing but praise for the pick and roll a la Utah Jazz, suggesting that even a play so disciplined and ancient was not predictable in their hands.

"It is perfected," Jordan said, "from the pass to the anticipation of when it's going to happen. At any given time, it may happen. And when it happens at the last moment you expect it, it's still going to be run to perfection.
"That tells you how much they are in tune with each other when they run that play."

Was it more important to stop Stockton or Malone, Bulls coach Phil Jackson was asked. "I think they go hand and fist," he said. "The reality is that you're going to get burned if you try to do too much of either one."
But Sloan felt the pick and roll did not work well in Sunday's two-point loss to the defending champions. "No, they did a great job of taking us out of it. We didn't run it (much)."
Asked if that meant the Bulls had found the best way to defend against the play, Sloan said cagily: "It is if we don't adjust to it."
Sloan feels his team did not run up and down the court hard enough, and Stockton agreed, sort of.
"Maybe we were a little tentative as far as trying to get up and down with them," Stockton said.

"That was on an individual basis, I don't think that was the game plan, don't get in a running game with Chicago or anything like that. But guys on a man to man basis might say, well, this shot might not be the best shot, we'll wait for our offence (to set up).

"We've been an opportunistic team all year, whether it's on the break or the set-up offence. So hopefully we'll make the right decisions -- if we have shots early we'll knock them down, if we don't we'll bring it out and run the offence."
Even if that means the boring old pick and roll.
